Reviewer Expertise:

Visual Identities, Visual Culture, Visual Communication Design

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard.

The article "Internal Perspectives on Visual Identities in Higher Education: A Case Study of Top-Ranked Universities in Indonesia" presents a comprehensive examination of the influence of visual identities (VI) on institutional reputation within higher education institutions (HEIs). Through semi-structured interviews with employees from five leading Indonesian universities, this study evaluates the role of VI through the Expressiveness Quotient (EQ), emphasizing dimensions such as visibility, distinctiveness, transparency, authenticity, and consistency. The findings suggest that effective management of VI aligns internal stakeholder perceptions with external branding, thereby enhancing competitive advantages and fostering cohesive organizational identities.

Constructive criticisms and recommendations 
                Depth of Theoretical Integration: This article would benefit from incorporating a more comprehensive theoretical framework by establishing connections between VI's impact and not only reputation but also specific academic outcomes or recruitment metrics, thereby providing a more substantive link to HEI performance.
                    Broader Empirical Evidence: While the case study approach provides in-depth insights, incorporating quantitative elements can enhance the generalizability of the findings. Subsequent research might consider employing surveys or experimental designs to validate qualitative insights on a larger scale.
                    Comparison with Global Standards: This study focuses on Indonesian universities but lacks a comparison with global practices. Incorporating examples or data from Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) in other regions could enhance the analysis and provide a benchmark for Indonesian universities.
                    Stakeholder Diversity: Expanding the range of interviewees to encompass external stakeholders, including students, alumni, and industry partners, could provide a more comprehensive perspective on how VI influences perceptions beyond the internal staff. To ensure the scientific validity of this article, addressing these issues is essential. Expanding the theoretical framework, implementing a mixed-methods approach, diversifying the participant base, and incorporating comparative global insights would substantially enhance the methodological rigor and generalizability of the research.

I had the pleasure of reviewing the manuscript entitled 
                Advances in Leukemia detection and classification: A Systematic review of AI and image processing techniques.

In the beginning, the manuscript presents thoroughly high-quality statistics of global epidemiology of leukemia and clarifies the leukemia subtypes and their diagnosis for the readers. The results provide a comprehensive overview of the advances in AI-assisted leukemia diagnosis, covering a significant amount of scientific literature published in this field.

In my opinion, weaknesses of the paper include the fact that it is not clear from the content and the structure of the manuscript the purpose of performing, at the same time, a review on risk factors, leukemia classification, and AI role in image processing for leukemia detection. It is mainly presented as a review of AI applications, though the methods sections and its subsections introduce the research on risk factors and leukemia classification as well, its role in the broader context of the paper being rather unclear.

The paper does not address any of the limitations of this systematic review. There might be an issue with the first line of section 
                4. Overview of AI in medical diagnostics, a part of the phrase or paragraph might be missing.

Reviewer Expertise:

Laboratory medicine (hematology, biochemistry, immunology, microbiology, molecular biology and genetics), medical bioinformatics

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard.

This manuscript presents a broad, PRISMA-guided systematic review and bibliometric analysis of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in leukemia, with a particular focus on image-processing and convolutional neural network (CNN)–based approaches for diagnostic support. The authors also summarise global epidemiology and risk factors, and devote a substantial section to updated classification frameworks (WHO-HAEM5 and ICC 2022) for the main leukemia entities (ALL, AML, CLL, CML).

The manuscript is timely and broadly informative, particularly in how it links AI applications to up-to-date WHO and ICC 2022 classification schemes. It has clear educational value for hematology clinicians who are not AI specialists.

There are methodological and scope-related limitations that, in my view, justify additional revision

- The “systematic review” component relies on a single database (Scopus) without formal risk-of-bias assessment or protocol registration. For a systematic review, this is a significant limitation, particularly in a field where many key AI and hematology papers are indexed in MEDLINE/PubMed and Embase but not always in Scopus. I recommend that the authors explicitly acknowledge the single-database constraint as a methodological limitation in the Methods and Limitations sections. If feasible, extending the search to at least MEDLINE/PubMed would strengthen the systematic nature of the work. Also, please clarify whether any language restrictions were applied.

- The manuscript does not report a formal risk-of-bias / quality assessment of AI diagnostic studies (e.g. PROBAST, TRIPOD-AI frameworks). Given the high risk of overfitting and spectrum bias in small, single-centre AI studies, this is a crucial missing element. At minimum, the authors should explicitly state that no formal risk-of-bias tool was applied and add a paragraph discussing how this may affect the reliability of reported performance metrics (particularly studies reporting >95–99% accuracy on small datasets).

- AI coverage is strongly image-centric, with minimal discussion of other clinically mature machine-learning approaches such as models based solely on routine complete blood count (CBC) and laboratory parameters, including large, externally validated tools such as AI-APL (PMID 38670741). Additional presentatin of these approach should be proposed.

- The current AI section presents an extensive catalogue of individual studies and reported accuracies (often >95–99%), but the synthesis remains largely descriptive. I would encourage the authors to Structure the synthesis by modality and task (e.g. blood smear / image, complete blood count, genomic ... and diagnosis vs outcome),

provide a higher-level summary table to precises Typical dataset sizes (n, centres, public vs single-institution), whether external validation was performed and key performance metrics and their clinical relevance (e.g. sensitivity for APL vs non-APL). and integrate Integrate a brief methodological critique. This would move the review from a “who did what” catalogue to a true critical synthesis, more in line with the article’s ambitions. Besides, reporting accuracies of more than 99% in biology should always be criticized.

- Other recent reviews in the field might be cited: the recent blood review for example (AI in Hematology, 2025)

The manuscript titled 
                “Advances in Leukemia detection and classification: A Systematic review of AI and image processing techniques” is well written, timely and relevant to the current trends in medical AI. It provides a clear and comprehensive synthesis of the literature on artificial intelligence applications for leukemia diagnosis, integrating epidemiological data, classification systems and machine learning approaches.

Strengths 
                The paper is methodologically solid and follows the PRISMA framework correctly.
                    The revision to include the WHO-HAEM5 (2022) and ICC (2022) classification updates adds strong clinical value and makes the review up-to-date.
                    The discussion section successfully links AI advances to modern hematopathological classifications and clinical practice guidelines (NCCN).
                    The figures and tables are informative and enhance readability.
                    The language is clear and accessible for both clinicians and data scientists. 
                Minor Points for Improvement 
                Clarity and conciseness: Some paragraphs (especially in the AI section) could be shortened or simplified to improve flow.
                    Discussion: Add a short paragraph summarizing key clinical implications and practical recommendations for integrating AI tools in real hospital workflows.
                    Formatting: Double-check spacing, alignment and numbering consistency (particularly in multi-column tables). 
                Recommendation

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard.

This thorough systematic review examines advances in AI and image processing techniques for leukaemia detection and classification. The authors analysed over 25k scientific articles from Scopus using PRISMA, focusing on ALL, AML, CLL, and CML. The review covers global epidemiological trends, risk factors, classification methods, and a comprehensive comparison of AI applications, particularly CNNs, for leukaemia diagnostics. The manuscript provides a detailed bibliometric analysis and evaluates various machine learning and deep learning approaches, discussing their performance metrics, limitations, and clinical applications.

With regards to the discussion, I believe that it would benefit from an additional brief section to explore how AI tools could be integrate into existing clinical workflows (i.e. at what point would said AI tools be integrated in a hypothetical EPR infrastructure, even as a thought experiment) and the barriers to implementation, ideally citing a real-world example.

Otherwise, I believe that this manuscript should be indexed.

As a hematopathologist, this review will be focusing on the the Section 3 (Classification of Leukemia).

The FAB morphological classifications used in this manuscript are very dated with limited therapeutic or prognostic values in the current standard of care. Please use the current WHO HAEM5 or ICC classification:

WHO Myeloid: [Ref 1]

WHO Lymphoid (For CLL and ALL): [Ref 2]

ICC Myeloid and acute leukemia (including AML, CML, and ALL): [Ref 3]

ICC Lymphoma (for CLL): [Ref 4]

The four disease groups selected for this manuscript were not a representative or related combination, although they were mostly-known diseases that bear the name "leukemia" (peripheral blood with or without marrow involvement), particularly for the two diseases with the "chronic" title.

CLL (or CLL/SLL) is a mature B cell lymphoma commonly with leukemic states. Other mature B- and T-cell neoplasms commonly presenting with leukemic state also include mantle cell lymphoma, hairy cell leukemia, splenic marginal zone lymphomas, T-PLL, T- or NK-LGLL, and many other disease entities.

CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN). Other MPN (such as CNL), MPN/MDS (such as CMML and atypical CML), and myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene rearrangements can also present with leukemic state (or cytosis).

For ALL, the L3 now is mostly Burkitt lymphoma (a mature B cell lymphoma), which can present as circulating abnormal "blast"-like cells.

For sections 5.2 and 5.3, as well as Figure 7 and 8, it would be helpful if the authors can compare your model with the those in the professional guidelines, such as the NCCN guidelines (nccn.org, free registration needed to download).

Although I am not an AI expert, the section 6 appears to be a laundry list of summaries of literature, without necessary integration. Instead, the authors should propose a list of items and use the literature to substantiate.

In other words, did any experts review the questions with your purpose statement to ensure they are valid and will result in effective results? For example, you ask about “good vision”. This is so subjective I would never use such a subjective term. If you did not validate these questions you need to add this issue to the limitations of this study. If only one person generated the questions there is certainly bias.
                    Pg. 4 this sentence “All participating children were proficient in English and did not have any impairments apart from vision” do not say impairments say disabilities.

You need to look up what qualitative research is and then revise this study.
                    Under results do not say “normal vision” just say vision. Also, if 34% had no VI then why were they in the study?
                    Pg. 13 you state “For children to perform well, effective eyehand coordination, clear vision, and good depth perception are crucial visual abilities.” This is not true. There are many blind sports such as goalball, blind tennis, and blind soccer to name a few that require no vision. You say this several times throughout the manuscript. You need to change this belief as it is just not true. These are international sports so they are available to these children.
                    Your discussion highlights several important points, such as isolation and loneliness, the need for sports, and more. These insights could have emerged with a more in-depth analysis of your data, which would have allowed for a richer exploration of these themes in your paper
                    I suggest you forgo the need to try to fit this data into an existing list of criteria. Instead use the data you found and truly develop themes and subthemes so you can share the reality of the lived experiences of the participants. As this study reads now, the research questions used are not validated and you used the voices of the experts and the children to try and force them into an existing instrument. This is not the intention of qualitative research. Unless these researchers revise the manuscript to better reflect the voices of the children involved, its contribution to the literature may be limited. The effort is clearly present; now, it would be valuable to focus on listening to the participants and sharing their perspectives more fully.

Summary: The study is an addition of evidence to the existing literature on the importance of assessment of the quality of life of Children with visual impairment. Details related to responses given as "Partly::

Methods: The categorisation of statements to different  domains/subscale and the classification of statements based one emotional tone is mentioned under the steps  followed. However, additional details on how this is ensured among the two individuals involved in allocating the responses to different domains may be required. It may give information about ensuring standardisation among the people and also will tell on how the disagreements between the coders is resolved while assigning the domains and assigning the comments to positive, negative or neutral. Parents, an important part of children's daily life are not included into the group discussions. A few lines mentioning the rationale for not including parents may be useful.

It helps to give a clear understanding on the outcomes of the discussions based on the categories versus the responses. This may be a basis to develop the tool for children to measure the impact, as given in conclusion.

Discussion: The importance of the results and how it helps in giving a basis for the requirement of a separate tool may be brought into the discussion. It will strengthen the idea of developing the items of the questionnaire.

Cultural landscape

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard.

Thoroughness & Scope – The article provides an extensive review of historical, cultural, and scientific aspects of the Konark Temple’s construction. The depth of research and integration of multiple sources, including historical texts, archaeological findings, and indigenous knowledge, is commendable.

Interdisciplinary Approach – The combination of historical analysis, engineering insights, and cultural narratives enriches the discussion. However, a more structured comparison with contemporary temple architecture across different regions of India could provide additional context.

Scientific and Engineering Aspects – The discussion on iron usage and rust-resistant techniques is fascinating. It would be helpful to include a comparison with other ancient iron structures, such as the Iron Pillar of Delhi, to establish technological linkages.

Specific Comments:

Historical Narratives & Myths – While the study effectively explores historical accounts and folklore, some claims (such as the floating deity using magnets) require additional corroboration from scientific sources or metallurgical studies.

Methodology Clarification– The systematic review method is well described, but the inclusion criteria for selecting historical texts, palm leaf manuscripts, and indigenous narratives should be elaborated. How were these sources validated for accuracy?

Illustrations & Figures – The inclusion of figures is helpful in visualizing the temple’s architectural layout. However, some of them lack detailed captions or references to their sources (e.g., Figure 5’s sketch of the temple in its complete state).

Construction Techniques & Materials– The identification of Khondalite, Laterite, and Chlorite stones is insightful. However, the decay rate comparison with Western structures like St. Paul’s Cathedral might need more quantitative backing with geological studies.

Maritime & Transportation Hypothesis– The theory of stone transportation via sea routes is intriguing. Have geological or sedimentary studies been conducted along these proposed routes to confirm ancient maritime trade or transport links?

References: Lafta Farhan S.et.al. 2022 (Ref 1) This study discusses the transformation of historical city centers and could provide a comparative perspective on the cultural and architectural sustainability of heritage sites, similar to the preservation efforts and architectural significance discussed in the Konark Temple study.

The Konark Temple’s Construction: A Critical Review of the Historical, Cultural, and Scientific Evidence

Summary of the Article

The article critically reviews the historical, cultural, and scientific evidence surrounding the construction of the Konark Temple in Odisha, India. The research incorporates data from ancient texts, folklore, palm leaf manuscripts, archaeological evidence, and historical records. It explores themes such as the temple's purpose, the techniques and materials used, the role of indigenous knowledge, and its architectural and astronomical precision.

Key findings include: 
                The temple served as a monument of devotion to the Sun God and a symbol of King Narasimhadeva I’s military victories.
                    Advanced construction techniques included using rust-resistant iron, innovative stonelifting technologies, and precise architectural designs.
                    The temple's alignment with astronomical phenomena demonstrates ancient artisans' mastery of astronomy.
                    Indigenous technologies, including the use of high-grade iron and efficient transportation of massive stone blocks via sea routes, highlight the engineering ingenuity of the time. The article concludes that the Konark Temple embodies a blend of artistic mastery, cultural significance, and technological innovation, offering insights for contemporary architecture and engineering.

Evaluation and Recommendations

1. Comprehensiveness of the Topic in Current Literature

Evaluation:

This is a rapid multi-stage scoping review and mini-meta-analysis aimed at identifying potential interventions for preventing cognitive decline in patients with cSVD which could be tested in a phase-3 platform trial. Pre-clinical and clinical studies were screened. Potential interventions were filtered down to 10 by removing duplicates and those interventions deemed ineffective (including non-cost-effective ones) or unavailable. The shortlisted candidate interventions for cSVD were assessed in mini-meta-analyses, and phosphodiesterase5-inhibitors showed higher OR. These ten shortlisted interventions were further narrowed down to three by an independent scientific advisory committee that prioritised metformin, tadalafil, and ISMN.

This is a well-structured and well-written straight-forward and practical scoping review of experts in the field of CSVD and vascular dementia, aimed at guiding future research and fostering purposeful clinical trials. This review contributes significantly to the field by focusing on repurposing existing drugs, which may lead to faster and more cost-effective future trials. I have only a minor questions/comment:

The authors clearly state that the study aims to identify promising drugs suitable for phase-3 testing in the UK and acknowledge this location-specificity as a limitation, given that drugs available elsewhere may be excluded. Could the authors comment on how restricting the analysis to UK-authorized drugs and excluding “impossible or impractical interventions” might affect the generalizability of the findings to other countries, particularly low- and middle-income settings where CSVD burden is highest? From my perspective, these restrictions may not diminish, and could potentially enhance, the applicability of the results to resource-limited contexts with constrained research funding and healthcare infrastructure. The authors’ insights on this would be valuable.

The annotation guidelines are necessary for the alignment of the  annotators, to decrease the inter-annotator error, for the validation of the procedures and are useful for other to be able to do a similar exercise in the future. An example (in spanish: https://zenodo.org/records/6477407).

In many senses, they are the most important legacy of any annotation process. This publication comes halfway to provide the information for the annotation handbook.

2.- Regarding manual curation. where are the numbers of raw identifications and the number of articles rejected and  for what reasons?

This information will  be very interesting to better understand how effective the text mining was and what are the main source of problems.

3.- The authors discuss the limitations of the study including the access to non-open literature. This is true, but it is also true that the grants are quoted, at least in part, in the Medline entries. Is this information used? or only from full open paper in EuroPMC? and if not, why not?

4.- Table 2 with the sources of publications is important, but it does not give the numerical information on how many articles were extracted with each query and what was the overlap ?  This information will be important to understand the influence of the different sources and to plan future experiments.

5.- I find difficult to understand the section dedicated to the retrieval of "key articles" and how articles quoting an ELIXIR resource were processed to identify contribution of ELIXIR-IT. Where the articles quoting key resources considered part of the ELIXIR-IT contribution even if they did not acknowledge a specific grant?

6.- Related with the previous point. The case study is interesting but I find the analysis of the data insufficient.

Apparently, a quarter of the ELIXIR citations are from publications "solely" by ELIXIR.-IT? this seems to be too many, and likely many of the ELIXIR publications are derived from collaborations between ELIXIR-IT and other ELIXIR nodes.

What is the overlap? how many are unique ELIXIR-IT publications? and to what do they correspond (areas of elixir? Core tools produce in Italy - detailing what is given  in Fig 5?)

7.-The problem with the umbrella institutions is well known. In other cases, efforts have been made to disambiguate the affiliations to increase granularity by, for example, using the other addressed in the same paper.

8.- Fig 2. legend is publications and citations but only citations are shown.

9.- I do not understand how table 5 was generated. HOw the articles (how many?) dedicated to the core resources are assigned to the platforms? How many papers and citations have each one of them?

10.- Table 5. Will be correct to say that the Italian core resources were quoted 1426 times in 2022 and that in total publications of ELIXIR-IT were quoted 1910 times this year?I If this is the case, it will be important to discuss this point: the main source of impact of ELIXIR are the core resources and not the work in the grants (75% of the citations) right?  Is this the case of ELIXIR or only for ELIXIR-IT?

11.- After making a selection of papers by grants, and even if not all the papers quote the corresponding grant, it will be very interesting to provide and discuss what grants have been quoted more often- and in this sense have been more influential.

12.- Overall, It is. a pity that the paper provides such a shallow level of analysis. For example, the overall number of papers and citations, does not really help to understand the impact of ELIXIR or ELIXIR-IT.  Providing number without a context does not really advance the analysis of impact and legacy.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

This manuscript presents an approach to identifying and measuring the scientific impact of ELIXIR-supported publications, employing text-mining of EuropePMC alongside manual curation. It offers valuable insights into the output and influence of a distributed research infrastructure, with an in-depth case study of ELIXIR Italy. The methodology is generally sound and relevant; however, several clarifications are needed to ensure transparency and reproducibility.

Major Concerns:

* The authors should include concrete examples (e.g., sample URLs or code snippets) illustrating how EuropePMC’s API was queried and how retrieved data were processed. This addition would strengthen reproducibility.

* A subset of known ELIXIR-supported articles had to be manually whitelisted, suggesting certain limitations in the automated text-mining. The authors are encouraged to explain why these articles failed to appear in the initial searches (e.g., unusual acknowledgments or missing metadata), as such detail would be instructive for others employing similar methods.

Minor concerns:

* The figure 2 indicates ~6,721 citations, whereas the text mentions 5,000. This discrepancy should be resolved for clarity.

* According to the text, 408 unique publications were supported by ELIXIR Italy from 2015 to 2023. Figure 3 shows the distribution of these publications across the Node’s institutes. If one sums the values for all institutes in Figure 3, the total appears to be 772, which does not match 408. The authors should clarify whether Figure 3 double-counts papers co-authored by multiple institutes or if other factors account for the difference.

The manuscript is well-structured, and the research offers a promising approach for tracking the impact of distributed infrastructures. Addressing the concerns above will strengthen the paper’s clarity and transparency. I recommend minor revision prior to acceptance.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

This article describes a method to assess the impact of ELIXIR supported research. This was done by using text mining to search for relevant articles contained in EuropePMC. This procedure was used for all ELIXIR nodes and for ELIXIR Italy. In the latter case the search terms were modified to be appropriate for that node. In the first step specific search terms were used to search sections of articles. This automated procedure was followed by manual curation.

It is important to have quantitative methods to analyze impact of the ELIXIR infrastructure and this is a good first step. The paper is well written, and the limitations of the approach are adequately described. For example, the EuropePMC does not index all the journals that describe projects funded under the ELIXIR umbrella. It is also disturbing that some articles are published in journals that are behind paywalls.

Although the curated datasets are put into Zenodo, the authors might consider making a website that would allow authors to submit and curate their ELIXIR related articles.
